newsitem.title: DUBAI: Lawyers deny demanding crucifixion of U.K. nurses.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers deny demanding crucifixion of U.K. nurses.

text.p: Lawyers representing the family of an Australian nurse murdered in Saudi Arabia denied they had demanded the two British nurses accused of her murder be crucified after execution.

Some Gulf newspapers on Monday published reports alleging the victim's family and lawyers had requested that Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, be crucified after execution "because they robbed and killed Yvonne Gilford".
"We categorically deny these reports," The International Law Firm representing the Gilfords said in a statement, faxed to Reuters from the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Parry and McLauchlan are accused of murdering Yvonne Gilford, an Australian colleague, at the King Fahd military medical complex where all three worked.
Gilford, 55, was found stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated in her room at the medical complex in the nearby oil city of Dhahran.
If Parry and McLauchlan are found guilty of murder, they could face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally public beheading by the sword.
Crucifixion of the executed criminal's body is established in Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom but not known to have been used recently.
The trial which resumed at Khobar sharia court on Sunday, adjourned after one hour. Sources close to the case said the trial would resume on August 10.
"The Gilford family has indicated that it would not waive the death penalty in the event that one or both of the defendants are convicted of intentional murder," the statement said.
"At no time has the Gilford family or The International Law Firm demanded crucifixion," it added.
According to sharia law, the victim's family may demand the death penalty if the court finds the two women guilty and says capital punishment is appropriate.

The Law firm Salah al-Hujailan, representing Parry and McLauchlan, said on Sunday the court was now leaning towards disqualifying the family of Yvonne Gilford from any role in determining the fate of the two nurses.

The court had initially questioned whether the power of attorney granted by the victim's mother Muriel Gilford, 84, to her son was valid. Muriel suffers from Alzheimer's disease and lives in a nursing home in Australia.
The power of attorney gives Frank Gilford, the victim's brother, the right to speak on behalf of the victim's closest family -- made up of their mother and himself.
The Sharia court ruled earlier that Frank Gilford could speak for the family, giving him the right to demand execution if the alleged killers of his sister were found guilty.
Parry and McLauchlan have withdrawn confessions which they said they were forced into making. Both say they are innocent.
